cards: Frederick Barbarossa was Holy Roman Emperor in the twelfth century.
John, King of England from 1199, was the youngest son of Henry II.
Henry the Lion was a Welf prince, Duke of Saxony from 1142 and Duke of Bavaria from 1156, the most powerful German noble of his age.
Henry II of England, the first Plantagenet king, ruled England, Normandy, Anjou and, through his wife Eleanor, Aquitaine, a block of lands known as the Angevin Empire.
Richard I of England, known as Richard the Lionheart, was King of England from 1189 to 1199 and a leading commander of the Third Crusade.
Andrei Bogolyubsky was the son of Yuri Dolgoruky and Grand Prince of Vladimir from 1157.
Pope Innocent III, born Lotario dei Conti di Segni, led the Church from 1198 to 1216 and was one of the most powerful medieval popes.
Afonso I of Portugal, known as Afonso Henriques, was the first king of Portugal.
Otto I of Wittelsbach was a Bavarian count palatine and a loyal follower of Frederick Barbarossa, whom he served on campaigns in Italy.
Roger II was Count of Sicily from 1105, then united the Norman lands of southern Italy by taking Apulia and Calabria, Capua, Bari and Naples.
Alfonso I of Aragon, known as the Battler, was king of Aragon and Navarre in the early twelfth century.
Bakhtiyar Khalji was a Turkic-Afghan commander of the Ghurids who conquered Bihar and western Bengal at the end of the 12th century.
Ramon Berenguer IV, Count of Barcelona
Ramon Berenguer IV was Count of Barcelona from 1131.
Albert the Bear was a prince of the Ascanian house who received the Northern March from Lothair III in 1134.
Alfonso II was the son of Ramon Berenguer IV of Barcelona and Petronila of Aragon.
Boniface I, Marquis of Montferrat, was the leader of the Fourth Crusade, which captured Constantinople in 1204.
Muhammad al-Idrisi was an Arab geographer and cartographer, born probably in Ceuta, who worked at the court of the Norman king Roger II of Sicily in Palermo.
Tamar was queen regnant of Georgia from 1184 to 1213, and her reign marks the height of the medieval Georgian kingdom.
Vishnuvardhana was a king of the Hoysala Empire in southern India, ruling from about 1108 to 1152.
Abd al-Mu'min was the first caliph of the Almohad Caliphate, proclaimed caliph c. 1133 as successor to the movement's founder Ibn Tumart.
proclaimed caliph c. 1133 · Egypt & North Africa
Alfonso VIII was king of Castile from 1158 to 1214.
Bolesław III Wrymouth was duke of Poland from 1102 to 1138.
David IV of Georgia, known as the Builder, became king in 1089 and stopped paying tribute to the Seljuks.
Ibn Tumart was a Berber religious reformer who preached a strict doctrine of the unity of God and proclaimed himself the Mahdi.
Arthur of Brittany was the posthumous son of Geoffrey, son of Henry II of England, and Constance, duchess of Brittany.
Averroes, or Ibn Rushd, was an Andalusian philosopher, physician and judge of the twelfth century who served the Almohad caliphs.
Bijjala II was the most important ruler of the Kalachuris of Kalyani in the Deccan.
Wanyan Aguda was the founder of the Jurchen Jin dynasty and its first emperor, known as Taizu, ruling from 1115 to 1123.
Gerard of Cremona was an Italian scholar who worked in Toledo and translated scores of Arabic scientific and philosophical works into Latin.
Niklot was prince of the Obotrites, a West Slavic people on the Baltic coast of what is now Mecklenburg.
Nizami Ganjavi was a Persian poet from Ganja in the Caucasus, regarded as the greatest master of the romantic epic in Persian.
Ong Khan, born Toghrul, was khan of the Keraites in central Mongolia and a sworn brother of Temüjin's father.
Absalon was a Danish churchman and statesman, Bishop of Roskilde and later Archbishop of Lund, and the chief adviser of King Valdemar I.
Alfonso VII of León and Castile
Alfonso VII was King of León and Castile from 1126 and was crowned Emperor of All Spain in 1135.
Basava, also called Basavanna, was a 12th-century Kannada poet, philosopher and social reformer and a minister at the court of the Kalachuri ruler Bijjala II at Kalyani.
Godfrey I of Louvain, called the Bearded, was Count of Louvain and Brussels and, from 1106, Duke of Lower Lorraine.
Louis VII was King of the Franks from 1137 to 1180, of the Capetian dynasty.
Hasan-i Sabbah was an Ismaili missionary who founded the Nizari branch after the succession crisis of 1094 in the Fatimid Caliphate.
Mstislav I, called the Great, was Grand Prince of Kiev from 1125 to 1132, the eldest son of Vladimir Monomakh and Gytha of Wessex.
Owain Gwynedd, son of Gruffudd ap Cynan, ruled Gwynedd from 1137 and made it the leading Welsh power.
